paragraphs: 3D-VLA connects three-dimensional perception, language reasoning, and action through a model that can generate representations of future goals. The paper addresses two gaps in earlier vision-language-action systems: their reliance on two-dimensional inputs and their direct mapping from observations to actions. Its approach brings the surrounding physical world and its dynamics into the same framework as action prediction.

The system builds on a language model designed for 3D information and adds action tokens for interaction with an embodied environment. The researchers also train diffusion models and align them with the language model so that the system can predict goal images and point clouds. They construct its training data by extracting 3D information from existing robotics datasets.

Experiments on held-in datasets report significant improvements in reasoning, generation across modalities, and planning. These findings support combining action capabilities with the generation of possible goal states. The reported evaluation concerns held-in data; the abstract presents real-world use as a promising application of these capabilities.
icml-2024-3d-vla-a-3d-vision-language-ac.tldr: 3D-VLA combines 3D perception, language, action tokens, and diffusion-based goal generation to improve embodied reasoning and planning on held-in datasets.

paragraphs: This paper studies how a model should preserve and update knowledge while learning a sequence of linear regression tasks. It focuses on regularization: restrictions on updates that influence how strongly learning a new task changes earlier knowledge. The reference point is an oracle estimator that can access every task's data simultaneously, providing a statistical benchmark for sequential learning.

The researchers analyze a family of generalized squared penalties controlled by matrix-valued settings. This family includes minimum-norm estimation and continual ridge regression. They derive a recursive expression for estimation error as tasks arrive, then use it to identify optimal settings. Those settings balance knowledge transfer between earlier and later tasks while accounting for differences in their data.

The optimal method achieves estimation error of the same order as the oracle, while lower bounds establish that the two named special cases are suboptimal in this analysis. The paper also establishes an equivalence between early stopping and generalized regularization in its continual-learning setting. Experiments complement these theoretical results.
icml-2024-a-statistical-theory-of-regula.tldr: For sequential linear regression, appropriately chosen matrix-valued regularization achieves oracle-order estimation error while balancing knowledge transfer across tasks.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning methods often judge an updated policy by its expected performance. That average can improve without providing control over particularly poor outcomes. This paper addresses that distinction within trust-region, on-policy learning, where the authors argue that existing methods emphasize expected gains without adequately controlling the lower end of performance.

The central contribution is an objective whose optimization guarantees monotonic improvement in a lower probability bound on performance with high confidence. This makes the protected quantity a probabilistic performance bound, rather than an unconditional promise about every individual run. The authors turn that theoretical objective into Absolute Policy Optimization, or APO, and an efficient variant called Proximal Absolute Policy Optimization, or PAPO.

Experiments cover continuous-control benchmarks and Atari games. The authors report that both methods significantly outperform leading policy-gradient approaches, improving worst-case performance as well as expected performance. The findings indicate that explicitly targeting a high-confidence lower bound can support stronger average results while also addressing poor outcomes in the evaluated tasks.
icml-2024-absolute-policy-optimization-e.tldr: APO targets a high-confidence lower performance bound and empirically improves both worst-case and expected reinforcement-learning performance.

paragraphs: Guidance lets diffusion models steer generated samples more strongly toward a requested condition. A common approach combines model predictions linearly, with a guidance scale controlling the strength of that steering. This paper argues that the combination neglects nonlinear effects that become significant at large guidance scales, creating a mismatch with the underlying diffusion process.

The proposed characteristic guidance adds a nonlinear correction to classifier-free guidance. Its guiding requirement is that the resulting model respect the Fokker–Planck equation, which describes how the diffusion process's probability distribution evolves. The correction follows from that mathematical requirement and can be used without additional training. It is also compatible with existing sampling methods.

Experiments report stronger expression of prompts' semantic characteristics and fewer irregularities in generated images. The method is also evaluated in applications spanning magnetic phase-transition simulation and latent-space sampling. These results support correcting the mathematical behavior of strong guidance as a way to improve sample control and quality across the studied settings.
icml-2024-characteristic-guidance-non-li.tldr: Characteristic guidance adds a training-free nonlinear correction that improves diffusion guidance at large scales by enforcing consistency with the diffusion equation.

paragraphs: Clifford-Steerable Convolutional Neural Networks build geometric symmetries into the way a convolutional model processes information. Their defining property is equivariance: transforming the input according to the relevant symmetry produces a corresponding transformation of the output. The paper develops this idea for multivector fields in pseudo-Euclidean spaces, giving one architectural framework for several different geometric settings.

The framework includes ordinary three-dimensional Euclidean symmetry and the Poincaré symmetry of Minkowski spacetime as particular cases. These examples connect the construction to both spatial and relativistic problems. To construct the required convolution kernels, the authors use an implicit parameterization based on Clifford-group-equivariant neural networks. The kernel construction therefore carries the symmetry requirements into the convolution operation.

The researchers evaluate these networks on forecasting tasks in fluid dynamics and relativistic electrodynamics. They report significant, consistent improvements over baseline methods in both areas. The findings provide empirical support for this shared geometric construction across the two tested physical settings, alongside the paper's broader architectural contribution.
icml-2024-clifford-steerable-convolution.tldr: Clifford-Steerable CNNs encode Euclidean and spacetime symmetries in a unified architecture and outperform baselines on two physical forecasting domains.

paragraphs: CompeteAI examines how language-model agents behave when they compete. Much work on multiple agents emphasizes collaboration, but competition introduces a different relationship: one agent's success can depend on attracting opportunities that other agents also want. The paper proposes a general framework for examining those dynamics and implements a concrete environment in which they can be observed.

The environment is a virtual town simulated using GPT-4, containing restaurant agents and customer agents. Restaurants compete to attract customers, creating pressure to change how they operate. The simulations examine how this pressure encourages the restaurant agents to develop new operating strategies, linking individual decisions to behavior across the simulated town.

The authors report findings at both individual and aggregate levels that align with existing market and sociological theories. They present the framework as a promising testbed for studying competition and its relationship to social behavior. The evidence concerns dynamics produced in this simulated environment, with the alignment to existing theories helping establish its value as a research setting.
icml-2024-competeai-understanding-the-co.tldr: CompeteAI uses GPT-4 restaurant and customer agents to study competitive adaptation in a virtual town, finding patterns aligned with market and sociological theories.

paragraphs: Replica exchange stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics is a sampling method used for large-scale, non-convex learning. The paper identifies a source of stagnation: its high-temperature chain can travel too far into the tails of the target distribution. Such excursions can undermine the exploration that this chain is meant to support, motivating explicit constraints on where sampling takes place.

The proposed reflected method, r2SGLD, keeps exploration within a bounded domain through reflection steps. Its theoretical analysis connects the size of that domain to mixing, or how efficiently the sampling process explores its distribution. The authors find that reducing the domain's diameter improves mixing rates with a quadratic relationship.

Experiments examine identifying dynamical systems with physical constraints, sampling constrained distributions with multiple modes, and image classification. Together, the theoretical and empirical results support bounded exploration as a way to improve simulation efficiency in the studied problems. The contribution is a sampling mechanism that makes constraints part of exploration and analyzes how domain size affects its behavior.
icml-2024-constrained-exploration-via-re.tldr: r2SGLD uses reflection to constrain sampling, with theory and experiments showing how bounded exploration can improve simulation efficiency.

paragraphs: A pretrained language model can retain a backdoor after ordinary fine-tuning, causing poisoned inputs to receive an attacker's chosen outputs. This creates a practical problem for downstream users: they may have clean task data but no knowledge of the attack strategy or its triggers. PURE is designed to mitigate backdoors under that information constraint.

The method combines two changes to the model's attention system. First, it uses only clean texts to identify and prune attention heads that are potentially affected by poisoned inputs. It then normalizes the attention weights of the remaining heads to further reduce backdoor effects. The two steps address both which heads remain and how their attention weights behave.

The authors evaluate PURE against several backdoor attacks on classification tasks. They report lower attack success rates without sacrificing performance on clean texts. This matters because a useful defense must reduce malicious behavior while preserving the model's intended task capability. The reported findings support that balance in the evaluated classification settings.
icml-2024-defense-against-backdoor-attac.tldr: PURE uses clean texts to prune suspicious attention heads and normalize remaining attention weights, reducing tested backdoor attacks while preserving clean-text performance.

paragraphs: Protein language models usually describe proteins at the residue level. That level of representation limits the atom-level information they can provide, which matters for applications involving proteins together with small molecules. ESM All-Atom, or ESM-AA, addresses this gap by bringing residue-scale and atom-scale molecular information into a unified modeling approach.

The model is pretrained on protein sequences that switch between the two scales. It also uses a position encoding designed to capture relationships among residues and atoms. These components give the pretraining process access to both levels of description and a way to relate them, making the relationship between molecular scales part of the learned representation.

Experiments report better performance than previous methods on protein–molecule tasks. Further investigations indicate that ESM-AA acquires molecular knowledge while retaining its understanding of proteins. That combination is central to the contribution: the model extends the scope of protein language modeling to finer molecular detail while preserving knowledge useful at the protein scale.
icml-2024-esm-all-atom-multi-scale-prote.tldr: ESM-AA unifies residue- and atom-scale pretraining, improving protein–molecule tasks while retaining protein knowledge.

paragraphs: In binary healthcare prediction, positive cases are often defined by specific medical criteria, while the negative category is more open-ended. The paper treats that negative category as a source of potentially meaningful patient groups. Its aim is to discover cohorts that could reveal information about the studied disease, related comorbidities, or complications.

The approach first assigns each sample a data Shapley value to quantify its contribution. It then constructs a Negative Sample Shapley Field describing the negative samples and their relationships. Manifold learning transforms this field while preserving essential structure and imposing an isotropy constraint on the Shapley values. Density-based clustering in the transformed space identifies candidate cohorts of medical interest.

The authors evaluate the approach using electronic medical records from Singapore's National University Hospital. They report clinically valuable insights consistent with existing knowledge. The result supports examining structure within negative cases rather than treating their shared label as the end of the analysis, with potential value for research and clinical decision-making.
icml-2024-exploiting-negative-samples-a-.tldr: The method combines data Shapley values, manifold learning, and clustering to uncover medically meaningful cohorts among negatively labeled patients.

paragraphs: GaLore tackles the memory required to train large language models, particularly the storage associated with optimizer states. Common low-rank adaptation methods freeze pretrained weights and train smaller added matrices. The paper instead proposes projecting gradients into a low-rank representation while allowing all model parameters to learn, preserving the scope of full-parameter optimization.

The authors evaluate GaLore on LLaMA 1B and 7B pretraining with C4 data, using up to 19.7 billion tokens, and on RoBERTa fine-tuning for GLUE. They report optimizer-state memory reductions of up to 65.5% while maintaining efficiency and performance. These findings concern memory savings during learning, alongside the ability to keep the full set of parameters trainable.

An 8-bit version reduces optimizer memory by up to 82.5% and total training memory by 63.3% relative to a BF16 baseline. The paper also demonstrates feasible pretraining of a 7B model on consumer GPUs with 24GB of memory, without model parallelism, checkpointing, or offloading. This establishes a concrete route to training within that memory budget.
icml-2024-galore-memory-efficient-llm-tr.tldr: GaLore projects gradients into low-rank form to reduce training memory while retaining full-parameter learning, enabling demonstrated 7B pretraining on 24GB consumer GPUs.

paragraphs: SEEACT explores whether a multimodal model can follow natural-language instructions to perform tasks on websites. It combines visual understanding with action selection and evaluates the result on MIND2WEB. The researchers also build tooling for testing agents on live websites, extending evaluation beyond cached pages to an online setting where actions must actually be executed.

A central finding separates planning ability from grounding: translating a textual plan into the correct website action. With manual grounding, GPT-4V completes 51.1% of live-website tasks, substantially outperforming the compared text-only and smaller specialized models. That result depends on human grounding and therefore measures capability under that assistance rather than fully automated task completion.

Automatic grounding remains the major obstacle. The paper finds that set-of-mark prompting is ineffective for these web-agent tasks, while its best developed strategy combines HTML structure with visual information. Even that strategy falls substantially short of oracle grounding. The findings identify a concrete gap between understanding what to do and reliably selecting the corresponding interface action.
icml-2024-gpt-4v-ision-is-a-generalist-w.tldr: SEEACT shows strong GPT-4V web-task capability with manual action grounding, while identifying automatic grounding as a major remaining bottleneck.

paragraphs: CLIP assigns a matching score to an image and a piece of text, but that score alone does not reveal which parts of either input influenced the match. Grad-ECLIP aims to explain a specific image–text pairing by producing heat maps that highlight influential image regions or words. The focus is interpretation of the matching result.

The method examines the encoder architecture and relates the final similarity score to intermediate spatial features. It applies channel and spatial weights to token features to construct visual explanations. This choice responds to a problem with attention-based explanations: CLIP's self-attention maps are typically extremely sparse, making them a difficult basis for informative attribution.

Qualitative and quantitative evaluations report better explanations than the compared state-of-the-art methods. The researchers also use those explanations to investigate how image–text matching works and to explore strengths and limitations in CLIP's attribution identification. The contribution therefore includes both an explanation method and an analytical tool for examining what contributes to a particular match.
icml-2024-gradient-based-visual-explanat.tldr: Grad-ECLIP explains image–text matches with gradient-based weighting of token features, producing stronger visual explanations in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Goal relabeling allows a reinforcement-learning agent to learn from an attempt that failed to achieve its original goal. This paper asks why that reuse can reduce the amount of experience needed for learning. It constructs an example demonstrating an information-theoretic improvement, providing a theoretical explanation for a technique already successful in practice.

The example shows how relabeling can extract richer information from observations by eliminating more hypotheses about the learning problem. Building on this insight, the authors introduce an algorithm called GOALIVE. They also define the goal-conditioned Bellman–Eluder dimension, a complexity measure designed to characterize the number of samples required in goal-conditioned reinforcement learning.

Compared with the existing Bellman–Eluder dimension, the goal-conditioned measure offers an exponential improvement in the best case. That qualification matters: the result establishes how large the benefit can be, rather than promising exponential savings for every task. Together, the construction, algorithm, and complexity measure connect the practical reuse of failed attempts to a formal account of sample efficiency.
icml-2024-how-does-goal-relabeling-impro.tldr: The paper explains goal relabeling through improved hypothesis elimination and develops GOALIVE with a complexity measure offering best-case exponential improvement.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning infers reward functions from an expert's demonstrations. This paper studies whether that inference can be performed efficiently, especially when learning must use previously collected data. In the offline setting considered, a behavior policy supplies the states and the expert policy supplies the actions; the behavior policy may itself be the expert.

The authors develop algorithms for both offline and online settings with polynomial sample requirements and runtime. Their analysis adapts the pessimism principle used in offline reinforcement learning, taking a conservative approach to uncertainty. They establish guarantees under stronger evaluation metrics than earlier work and derive lower bounds showing that their sample requirements are nearly optimal.

The paper also examines whether inferred rewards remain useful in another Markov decision process. It provides transfer guarantees when the target environment satisfies specified similarity assumptions relative to the source environment. Thus, the contribution addresses both efficient reward inference and conditional reuse of those rewards, with the transfer claim explicitly depending on similarity between the two environments.
icml-2024-is-inverse-reinforcement-learn.tldr: The paper gives efficient offline and online inverse-reinforcement-learning algorithms with nearly optimal sample complexity and reward-transfer guarantees under similarity assumptions.

paragraphs: Cell identity includes human-defined descriptions such as cell type, pathway information, and disease associations. Models trained only on transcriptomic measurements do not directly learn the language connecting those measurements to these descriptions. The paper identifies this as a problem when a downstream task has few labeled examples or lacks examples carrying the desired semantic labels.

LangCell addresses the gap during pretraining by learning a unified representation of single-cell data and natural language. Its text inputs contain information about cell identity, allowing the model to connect biological measurements with meaningful descriptions before task-specific fine-tuning. The key change is to make cell-identity knowledge part of cross-modal pretraining.

Across the reported benchmarks, LangCell is the only evaluated single-cell pretrained model that works effectively in zero-shot cell-identity settings. It also significantly outperforms existing models in few-shot and fine-tuning settings. These findings support pairing transcriptomic data with informative language as a way to improve cell-identity understanding when task-specific labeled data is scarce or unavailable.
icml-2024-langcell-language-cell-pre-tra.tldr: LangCell jointly pretrains on single-cell data and cell-identity text, enabling effective zero-shot understanding and improving few-shot and fine-tuned results in the reported benchmarks.

paragraphs: Cooperating agents can settle into a poor joint strategy because each learns around the others' current, suboptimal behavior. The paper calls this relative overgeneralization. It addresses the problem in multi-agent policy-gradient methods, where an agent's updates can reinforce premature commitment to a locally attractive strategy before better coordination develops.

The proposed framework makes updates optimistic by clipping negative advantage values to zero. Advantage values guide whether behavior should be encouraged or discouraged; removing the negative part changes how strongly disappointing outcomes push learning away from a choice. The authors argue that this optimism prevents agents from converging too quickly to a local optimum. Their formal analysis also shows that the method retains optimality at a fixed point.

Evaluations include Multi-agent MuJoCo and Overcooked tasks. The method outperforms strong baselines on 13 of 19 tasks and matches them on the remaining six. These results support a simple update modification for alleviating relative overgeneralization across the tested cooperative settings, alongside the stated fixed-point analysis.
icml-2024-optimistic-multi-agent-policy-.tldr: Clipping negative advantages enables optimistic multi-agent policy updates that alleviate relative overgeneralization and improve 13 of 19 tested tasks.

paragraphs: Premier-TACO aims to make learning a new control policy possible with only a small amount of expert demonstration data. It first learns a general visual representation from a subset of offline datasets spanning multiple tasks. That representation is intended to capture important environmental dynamics, giving later task learning a useful starting point.

The method extends temporal action contrastive learning, or TACO, by changing how negative examples are sampled during pretraining. Negative examples provide comparisons within the contrastive objective, so selecting them is part of how the representation is learned. The new sampling strategy substantially improves computational efficiency, making large-scale offline pretraining across multiple tasks feasible.

The pretrained representation is then fine-tuned using minimal expert demonstrations. Evaluations span DeepMind Control Suite, MetaWorld, and LIBERO, where the authors report significant improvements in few-shot imitation learning on novel tasks. The findings connect more efficient representation pretraining with reduced demonstration requirements during downstream learning, showing the value of reusing knowledge of dynamics across the evaluated control problems.
icml-2024-premier-taco-is-a-few-shot-pol.tldr: Premier-TACO makes multitask visual pretraining more efficient through negative-example sampling and improves imitation learning from few demonstrations on novel tasks.

paragraphs: PRISE treats the discovery of reusable action sequences as a compression problem. A temporal action abstraction groups behavior over time into a higher-level skill, allowing knowledge to be shared across sequential decision tasks. The paper asks whether a technique used to tokenize language can also identify useful skills with different durations in continuous-control problems.

Its method, Primitive Sequence Encoding, first quantizes continuous actions so they can be represented as discrete elements. It then applies byte pair encoding, the sequence-compression technique used in language-model tokenization, to learn action abstractions. Combining these steps connects continuously valued control actions to a method that operates on discrete sequences.

The researchers learn these skills from robotic manipulation demonstrations covering multiple tasks. Their experiments show significant improvements in downstream behavior-cloning performance when using the discovered high-level skills. This supports sequence compression as a practical way to extract transferable temporal structure from demonstrations, with the reported evidence centered on imitation learning for the evaluated robotic tasks.
icml-2024-prise-llm-style-sequence-compr.tldr: PRISE combines action quantization with byte pair encoding to discover variable-duration robotic skills that improve downstream behavior cloning.

paragraphs: Implicit neural representations describe a signal through a learned function, using a neural network to represent information such as an image or sound. A difficulty is capturing high-frequency components, which contain rapidly changing signal detail. The paper points to this challenge in conventional ReLU-based multilayer perceptrons and builds on Fourier Neural Networks as an alternative.

The proposed Quantum Implicit Representation Network, or QIREN, is a quantum generalization of Fourier Neural Networks. Its contribution therefore connects a signal-representation approach with quantum neural modeling. The authors provide theoretical analysis establishing a quantum advantage over classical Fourier Neural Networks, giving mathematical support for the proposed representation in addition to its experimental evaluation.

Experiments cover signal representation, image superresolution, and image generation. The authors report superior performance compared with state-of-the-art models on these tasks. Taken together, the theoretical comparison and empirical results identify implicit signal representation as a promising application for quantum neural networks, linking the proposed quantum construction to practical tests of representing and generating signals.
icml-2024-quantum-implicit-neural-repres.tldr: QIREN generalizes Fourier Neural Networks to a quantum model, with a theoretical quantum advantage and reported gains on signal and image tasks.

paragraphs: Machine unlearning aims to remove training data and its influence from an already trained model. This paper examines a security consequence of that process: removing information can increase a model's susceptibility to adversarial attacks, particularly when the original model was trained for adversarial robustness. Privacy-motivated model updates therefore introduce a security interaction worth examining directly.

The authors propose Adversarial Unlearning Attack, or AdvUA, which introduces a small fraction of malicious unlearning requests. In their findings, these requests significantly reduce the updated model's adversarial robustness relative to the original model. The attack exploits the unlearning process itself, creating an adversarial capability that the authors distinguish from attacks available in conventional training pipelines.

The paper also shows that AdvUA can strengthen model-stealing attacks by revealing additional information about decision boundaries. It includes theoretical and computational-complexity analyses, alongside numerical studies supporting the attack's effectiveness and efficiency. The results show that assessing an unlearning method's privacy function alone can miss changes to robustness and exposure to model extraction.
icml-2024-rethinking-adversarial-robustn.tldr: AdvUA shows that a small fraction of malicious unlearning requests can weaken adversarial robustness and strengthen model-stealing attacks.

paragraphs: Some segmentation targets depend strongly on their surroundings: recognizing camouflage, shadows, or lesions requires interpreting the relationship between foreground and background. Separate research communities have developed specialized models for these tasks. Spider brings them into one model with a shared parameter set, aiming to reduce the need for independently trained systems for each domain.

Spider uses a concept filter driven by a prompt consisting of grouped images and masks. This prompt helps the model determine which context-dependent concept the user intends to segment. The shared model is trained once and evaluated across eight tasks, covering salient, camouflaged, and transparent objects, shadows, and four kinds of medical lesions.

The authors report significant improvements over specialized state-of-the-art models across those tasks. They also examine adding new tasks: fine-tuning less than 1% of the parameters produces less than 5% performance degradation on all old tasks. These findings support both shared context-dependent segmentation and the ability to extend the model while limiting disruption to previously learned tasks.
icml-2024-spider-a-unified-framework-for.tldr: Spider uses image-and-mask prompts to unify eight context-dependent segmentation tasks and supports new tasks through limited parameter fine-tuning.

paragraphs: This paper improves language-model theorem proving by changing how demonstration examples are structured and presented. Demonstrations provide examples within the model's context, so their usefulness depends on both their content and their organization. The researchers focus on making intermediate proof goals explicit and choosing a helpful collection and ordering of examples.

The framework constructs distinct subgoals for each demonstration and refines them using ideas from subgoal learning in reinforcement learning and robotics. It then uses diffusion models to predict an organization of demonstrations, addressing subset selection and ordering together. These are complementary interventions: one changes the structure of each example, while the other changes which examples the prover sees and in what sequence.

On miniF2F, subgoal-based demonstrations raise proof accuracy from 38.9% to 44.1%. Adding diffusion-based organization can increase accuracy to 45.5%, or provide a fivefold improvement in sampling efficiency compared with established methods. The stated alternatives show that better demonstration organization can benefit either proof success or the sampling effort required.
icml-2024-subgoal-based-demonstration-le.tldr: Explicit subgoals and diffusion-based demonstration organization improve theorem-proving accuracy or sampling efficiency on miniF2F.

paragraphs: Long-tailed datasets contain many examples of common classes and relatively few examples of rare classes. Training strategies can therefore face a trade-off between performance on the frequent head classes and the scarce tail classes. This paper analyzes that trade-off theoretically and formulates it as a multi-objective optimization problem, making the competing performance goals explicit.

The authors then propose combining heterogeneous training strategies within that formulation. Combining strategies can introduce conflicts, so simply using several approaches together is not the whole solution. Their Multi-Objective Optimization based Strategy Fusion method, or MOOSF, is designed to resolve these conflicts and make the combination effective and efficient.

Experiments on mainstream datasets show that even a simple strategy combination can outperform complex long-tailed learning strategies. The findings support treating strategy interaction as an optimization problem in its own right. The paper's broader contribution is a way to reason about and coordinate competing training objectives, helping explain how relatively simple components can become effective when fused appropriately.
icml-2024-two-fists-one-heart-multi-obje.tldr: MOOSF frames head–tail performance trade-offs as multi-objective optimization and resolves conflicts when combining long-tailed learning strategies.

paragraphs: Gradient regularization adds a penalty on the gradient norm to the training loss. Although it can help train overparameterized networks, this paper finds that it can also degrade performance when used with adaptive optimizers, particularly during learning-rate warmup. The question is therefore how its strength interacts with the optimizer's behavior early in training.

Theoretical and empirical analyses suggest that the penalty can destabilize the gradient statistics accumulated by adaptive optimizers at the initial training stage. The researchers respond with three regularization-warmup strategies. Each relaxes the penalty during warmup to some extent, allowing gradient information to accumulate more accurately and stably before applying stronger regularization.

Experiments with Vision Transformer models show that the three strategies can avoid the identified problems and substantially improve performance. The authors also observe greater reliance on regularization warmup in more scalable models, reporting improvements of up to 3% on CIFAR-10 over baseline gradient regularization. The findings make early penalty scheduling a consequential part of using regularization with adaptive optimization.
icml-2024-when-will-gradient-regularizat.tldr: Gradient regularization can destabilize early adaptive optimization, and three warmup strategies mitigate this problem in Vision Transformer experiments.
